title: The book in hand

cards: A kid bursts out of the school gate on the last day of school, waving a report card over their head. Look! Read it!
They can't wait for someone to see. The Qur'an has a moment with that same joy in it, on the Day of Resurrection.
In Surah al-Haqqah, Pickthall's translation reads: "Then, as for him who is given his record in his right hand, he will say: Take, read my book!"

teach.h: KITAB: A WRITTEN RECORD OF EACH LIFE.
teach.b: The Qur'an speaks of a written record of each life, kitab, a book. Surah al-Infitar speaks of guardians, noble recorders, who know what people do. On the Day, the book is handed over.
In the right hand, joy: take, read my book. In al-Haqqah the next scene is the opposite.
The one handed the book in the left hand says, in paraphrase: I wish I had never been given my book, I wish I had never known my reckoning. Same plain, same book, two faces. And who reads it?
Surah al-Isra' answers, Pickthall again: "Read thy book. Thy soul sufficeth as reckoner against thee this day." You read your own.
Surah al-Kahf adds that those who see their books ask what kind of book this is, which leaves nothing out, small or great. Small things: a tone of voice, a held door.

If that were the whole picture it would be frightening, and here a hadith in Sahih al-Bukhari changes the arithmetic. The Prophet, peace be upon him, said that Allah wrote down good deeds and bad ones.
Whoever intends a good deed and doesn't do it, one full good deed is written for them. If they do it, ten, up to seven hundred times, or more.
Whoever intends a bad deed and holds back, that's written as a good deed; if they do it, it's written as one.
The book counts everything, and it counts generously. So it's a record, not a trap: there is still time to write in it.

how: Muslims believe angels record each person's deeds and that the record will be given to them on the Day of Resurrection, in the right hand or the left; the hope to receive it in the right hand appears in prayers and sermons.

games.q: what does “the book in hand” mean?
o: the book of laws a judge uses to settle a case in court
the record of each life, handed over on the Day and read by its owner
the Qur'an, the book every believer holds and recites daily

games.q: the book in hand — tap the pairs.
p: I wish I'd never been given it
nothing small or great left out

s: in the Qur'an, someone else reads your book out for you
al-Isra': "Read thy book. Thy soul sufficeth as reckoner against thee this day."
by a hadith in Bukhari, a good deed intended but not done is still written
one full good deed, and a bad deed held back is written as good.
the record only counts big deeds
al-Kahf: it leaves nothing out, small or great.

games.q: you meant to do a good deed today, and something stopped you. by the hadith in Bukhari, what's written?
games.why: intending a good deed and not doing it is written as one full good deed. doing it: ten, up to seven hundred times, or more.

practice: Find one good thing you've been meaning to do and haven't, small is fine, a visit you keep putting off, returning something you borrowed, and hold the intention clearly, because by the hadith the intention alone is already written.
Then picture yourself doing it, in a particular place, at a particular time. If you pray, you can ask that it be accepted.

wordCard.voice: The book in hand. The record of each life, given in the right hand or the left on the Day, and read by its owner. Today's word.

orig.note: Arabic: a book, a writing; here, the record of a life.

carryVoice: Your line: the book of deeds. Small things count, and good intentions too. Rest well.
